title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hook: a city where everyone is content, and the one man in it who isn't

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crow and the first verse, part two. Brahma told Valmiki the verse was meant, and two boys learned the whole poem by heart. Did you learn one line by heart? Now the story itself begins. Day four hundred ninety-five.

The first thing Valmiki gives us is a city. Ayodhya, on the river Sarayu, in the land of Kosala. He describes it lovingly: wide straight roads sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, gates and arches, music, merchants, horses, elephants, granaries full. In his telling, nobody there is greedy, nobody lies, nobody is without learning or without food. It's a picture of a city working as it should. And at the center of it sits a king who has everything, and who can't sleep for wanting the one thing he doesn't have.
screen: `AYODHYA, ON THE SARAYU.` → `A CITY WORKING AS IT SHOULD.` → `A KING WHO CAN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The king is Dasharatha, of the line of Ikshvaku. His name means ten chariots, and tradition explains it as one whose chariot could go in all ten directions. He's wise, generous, a famous warrior, guided by great counselors like the sage Vasishtha. He has three chief queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And he has no son. For a king in the epic's world, that isn't only personal sorrow. It's the line, the ancestors' rites, the kingdom's future. So Dasharatha thinks it through and decides: I will perform the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons. Notice how he does it. He doesn't act alone. He calls his priests and ministers, lays out his grief and his plan, and asks. And they approve. Then his charioteer and counselor, Sumantra, takes him aside with a story. Long ago, he says, he heard sages foretell this very moment: a king of Ikshvaku's line, longing for sons, would bring a certain young sage to his sacrifice, and sons would come. The sage's name is Rishyashringa. And Sumantra begins to tell who he is, a story strange enough that it'll take us all of tomorrow. So the Ramayana's first real scene isn't heroic at all. It's a good man, with everything, admitting what he lacks to the people around him, and asking for help.
screen: `DASHARATHA: TEN CHARIOTS.` · `THREE QUEENS, AND NO SON.` · `HE ASKS HIS COUNSELORS FIRST.` · `SUMANTRA REMEMBERS A PROPHECY.` · then, large: `THE HORSE SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let one longing come up, something you've wanted for a long time and don't have. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just hold it, the way Dasharatha held his, honestly. Then bring to mind one person you could tell about it, someone you trust. You don't have to call them. Just notice they're there. Breathe with the longing and the company together. The bell holds the time.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. The great horse sacrifice the childless king of Ayodhya decides on, with his counselors, for the sake of sons.
Your line: Dasharatha's sacrifice. Today, tell one person you trust about something you've been carrying alone, and ask what they think. Day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Ayodhya, on the Sarayu river in today's Uttar Pradesh, is revered in Hindu tradition as Rama's birthplace and is a place of pilgrimage; the Bala Kanda's opening chapters describe the city and its king.

myth: Dasharatha decides on the sacrifice without consulting anyone
he lays out his grief and plan to his priests and ministers first.
Sumantra links the moment to an old prophecy
a young sage named Rishyashringa will bring sons to the king.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. you have everything a king could want, except a son. what do you do?
options: decide on a great sacrifice, with your counselors' blessing.
go to war to win glory instead.
fork.reveal: he resolves on the ashvamedha for the sake of sons, and asks his priests and ministers first. they approve.

original.note: Sanskrit aśvamedha: the horse sacrifice, a great royal Vedic rite.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ramayana begins with Rama.
what it means: it begins with his father's longing, admitted honestly, and a decision made with others.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 5–8 describe Ayodhya and Dasharatha's court before the decision for the ashvamedha; Sumantra then tells of Rishyashringa, citing a prophecy he attributes to the sage Sanatkumara.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 5–7 (Ayodhya, Dasharatha, his counselors)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 8–9 (the decision for the horse sacrifice; Sumantra's prophecy)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common vulgate numbering; the Critical Edition differs.
The meaning 'ten chariots' and its explanation (a chariot that goes in ten directions) is a traditional gloss; confirm.
Valmiki's idealized city (no greed, no lies, no one unlearned) paraphrased from Bala Kanda 6; confirm.
The prophecy Sumantra recalls is attributed to Sanatkumara in the vulgate; confirm.
Editor review (2026-10-01): the ten-directions gloss on Dasharatha's name is now attributed to tradition; 'revered by many Hindus ... throughout the year' softened.
